AI in the Classroom, Right Here at GSU

An LLM club in our own department, three classroom ideas from Georgia Tech, and honest advice for assistant professors

This issue is about what is already happening close to home. A student and faculty group in our own department is meeting to explore large language models in depth. Across town, Georgia Tech faculty have published 67 detailed case studies of AI in teaching three translate directly to CS courses. And for newer faculty, a candid 7 part blog series on surviving the assistant professor years.

GSU CS · Student Initiative

There is already an LLM club in our department

The Large Scale Intelligence Club (LSIC) is a student led organization at GSU co advised by Dr. Murray Patterson from our own CS department. The club meets regularly to read papers, run experiments, and discuss the science and application of large language models including safety and interpretability.

If you teach anything touching NLP, machine learning, software engineering, or AI, this is a ready made community for your students. Joining is free through the Panther Involvement Network.

💡

Quick action: Mention LSIC to your students this semester, especially in upper division or graduate courses. A club that reads LLM papers is a natural extension of any course covering AI, NLP, or software engineering.

Georgia Tech · Academic AI Playbook 2026

Three classroom ideas from GT faculty worth trying

The GT Playbook we featured in Issue 1 contains 67 detailed faculty case studies. Below are three that are especially relevant for CS instructors. Each card includes the key outcome in one sentence, the original figure from the article, and a PDF download of the exact pages.

🤖
GT · Introductory Computing (CS1301: Introduction to Computing Principles)
BuzzTutor: AI tutoring that scaffolds instead of solves
An AI tutor deployed across GT intro CS courses that gives structured hints and Socratic questions instead of answers. When a student’s code fails, the system classifies the likely misconception and asks a guiding question rather than handing over a fix. Students can always escalate to a TA.
📊 900 students opted in voluntarily in the first year in CS1301 (Introduction to Computing Principles) alone, with no course requirement to do so.
What worked: Students who were prompted to explain their reasoning before receiving help learned more than those who received answers directly. Building in a moment of reflection turned out to matter more than the hint itself.
📄 Article PDF
⚙️
GT · Software Engineering (CS 3300) & Capstone
Beyond Vibe Coding: teaching AI as an engineering tool, not a shortcut
GT faculty embedded AI across the full software development lifecycle requirements, design, testing, debugging but required students to document every AI assisted decision and justify it against engineering principles. Students used multiple tools and compared AI assisted vs. manual workflows on the same tasks.
📊 Every confidence measure shifted upward post course including awareness of AI limitations and the importance of foundational coding knowledge.
What worked: The strongest students were not the ones who used AI the most. They were the ones who questioned its outputs, refined their prompts, and checked results against engineering principles. Requiring students to justify AI decisions in writing was the most effective accountability mechanism.
📄 Article PDF
📝
GT · Deep Learning (CS7643, 600 students)
Marginalia: an AI margin tutor embedded directly in lecture slides
A single HTML file tool no installation needed that lets students highlight any equation or figure in a lecture PDF and get a context aware explanation in the right margin. Each explanation starts with “Where you might get stuck” before any derivation. When a concept is dynamic, the tool generates an interactive animation on demand. Built using Claude via API in a few days.
📊 Early users reported understanding equations they had no handle on before, calling it a potential primary slide viewer for students.
What worked: Every tutorial opens with "Where you might get stuck" written from the student's point of view, before any derivation begins. Naming the specific confusion students are likely to feel turned out to be more valuable than the explanation that follows it. The prompt design is the pedagogical work; the architecture is secondary.
📄 Article PDF

For Assistant Professors · Recommended Reading

Honest advice from someone who just survived the tenure clock

Kenneth Hanson is an Associate Professor of Chemistry at Florida State University. After earning tenure in 2020, he wrote a candid 7 part blog series reflecting on his six years as an assistant professor what worked, what he wished he had known, and what nearly broke him. The writing is warm, practical, and genuinely funny.

Recommended by Samer Gozem, Professor of Chemistry at GSU. Read the posts from the bottom up (oldest to newest) for the full arc.

1
Part 1: Getting Started
Setting up your lab, ordering equipment, sole source justifications, getting your website online
2
Part 2: Research
Choosing a research direction, differentiating yourself from your advisor, building for the long term
3
Part 3: Management
Running your group, recruiting students, setting expectations, protecting your time
4
Part 4: Funding
Grant strategy, diversifying applications, navigating the funding landscape before tenure
5
Part 5: Gaining Prominence
Small focused conferences over large ones, working with your PR office, building your brand
6
Part 6: Teaching
Claiming a course, managing teaching load, separate email for students, using release time wisely
7
Part 7: Other
Finding community among junior faculty, work life balance, mental health, what actually mattered
